Geographic Themes (Three from the SL list)
HL Core Extension: Global Interactions (Power, Places & Networks; Human Development & Diversity; Global Risks & Resilience)

option-a-freshwater: At any moment, rivers hold only about 0.006% of Earth's fresh water. So how does a river keep flowing through weeks without rain?
option-b-oceans-coastal-margins: The Gulf Stream carries more water than all the world's rivers combined. Is that why north-west Europe has mild winters?
option-c-extreme-environments: Antarctica is covered in ice, yet it counts as a desert. How?
option-d-geophysical-hazards: The Atlantic is about 2.5 cm wider every year. What moves the plates?
option-e-leisure-tourism-sport: UK residents made about three times as many trips abroad as Indian nationals did in 2025, yet India has about 21 times as many people. Why?
option-f-food-health: In 2023 the world's food supply came to about 3,000 calories per person per day. So why did around 645 million people go hungry in 2025?
option-g-urban-environments: In Denmark, 200 people can make a place urban. In Japan it takes 50,000. So how urban is the world?
core-unit-1-changing-population: Why do more than 9 in 10 people in China live on one side of a single line?
core-unit-2-global-climate-vulnerability: In 1991 one volcano in the Philippines cooled the whole planet. How?
core-unit-3-global-resource-consumption-: In 1990, two in three people in East Asia and the Pacific lived in extreme poverty. By 2025, fewer than 1 in 50 did. So why did the number of extremely poor people in sub-Saharan Africa rise?
unit-4-power-places-networks: The Netherlands tops the KOF Globalisation Index. The USA, the world's largest economy at market exchange rates, ranks 28th. How can that be?
unit-5-human-development-diversity: Guyana's income per person is more than three and a half times Sri Lanka's. Why do they have exactly the same HDI?
unit-6-global-risks-resilience: On 12 May 2017, at least 81 of England's 236 NHS trusts were disrupted on the same day. Nobody broke into a single building. What happened?

option-a-freshwater: At any moment, rivers hold only about 0.006% of Earth's fresh water. So how does a river keep flowing through weeks without rain?
A silt grain is one-hundredth the width of a coarse sand grain, yet water must flow about three times as fast to pick it up. Why?
Niagara Falls has moved about 7 miles (11 km) upstream in about 12,000 years. How does a waterfall move backwards?

On 23 December 2013, 43–45 mm of rain fell on two river basins in southern England. Within a day, one river surged to one of its highest flows since records began; the other barely rose, and peaked only in mid-February after weeks more rain. Why did the same storm have such different effects?
A study found that urbanization made Hurricane Harvey-scale flooding in Houston's basins about 21 times as likely in 2017. How can a city make a flood worse?
In 1995, more than 250,000 people in the Netherlands had to leave their homes as the rivers rose. The Dutch response was not simply higher dikes. What did they do?
In January 2018 Cape Town, a city of just over 4 million people, warned that its taps could be turned off in April: "Day Zero". What pushed it to the edge, and how did it pull back?

Every summer, parts of Chesapeake Bay, USA, become "dead zones" with too little oxygen for fish and shellfish. Much of the cause starts on land, in a watershed spanning six states. How can a farm field suffocate a bay?
The Aral Sea was once the fourth-largest lake in the world. In 2014 the eastern part of its southern basin disappeared completely. What drained it?
About 85% of the Nile's water starts in Ethiopia, yet a 1959 agreement shared it between Egypt and Sudan. Who decides how it is used now, and what would make a deal work?

The Lower Mekong's fisheries land an estimated 2.3 million tonnes of fish a year, worth about US$11 billion. Its hydropower capacity could more than double. Can one river be both a great fishery and a giant power station?
Since 1970 the world has lost about 22% of its wetlands. Can a plan for a whole river basin bring a wetland back?
option-b-oceans-coastal-margins: The Gulf Stream carries more water than all the world's rivers combined. Is that why north-west Europe has mild winters?
In December 2023 the Panama Canal let through 22 ships a day, against 36 in its "regular scenario". What did a patch of warm Pacific Ocean have to do with it?
Hurricane Ian hit Florida with 130-knot winds in 2022. Why was water, not wind, its deadliest hazard?
The ocean took up 29% of the CO₂ humans emitted over the last decade. Why is that bad news for coral reefs?
Between 1951 and 2004 the cliffs at Aldbrough, on England's Holderness coast, retreated about 2 m a year. Why do they disappear so fast?
Spurn Point is over three miles long and in places only 50 m wide. How did a finger of sand form across the mouth of the Humber?
On the coast of the Gulf of Bothnia, the land rises out of the sea by about 0.9 m a century. Elsewhere, coasts are drowning. How can both be true?
By 2014 the Environment Agency had built new banks inland at Medmerry, West Sussex, and let the sea flood the land between. Why give land to the sea?
1,282 people and organisations sent formal comments on one plan for the Suffolk coast. Who were they, and who won?
A community on Kenya's coast earns money by not cutting down its mangroves. Who pays, and why?
The world now farms more fish and shellfish than it catches. Does that solve overfishing?
Tankers spilled about 95% less oil in the 2010s than in the 1970s. Why has plastic proved so much harder to stop?
Russia, Denmark and Canada have each asked a UN body to recognise their seabed rights in the Arctic Ocean. Who owns the ocean floor?
In 2024, ships from Shenzhen to Rotterdam began sailing about 3,000 extra nautical miles around Africa. Why take the long way?
option-c-extreme-environments: Antarctica is covered in ice, yet it counts as a desert. How?
Many people in the Australian opal town of Coober Pedy live in homes dug into rock. Why live underground?
Between 1941 and 2004, Alaska's Muir Glacier retreated 12 km. All that time, its ice kept flowing towards the sea. How can both be true?
A 16,500-tonne boulder sits on the flat prairie of Alberta, Canada, far from the mountains it came from. How did it get there?
Near Tuktoyaktuk in Arctic Canada, a 49 m hill rises out of flat tundra. Its core is solid ice. How did it form?
Sand covers only about 20% of the world's deserts. What shapes the rest?
From the 1960s, irrigation turned Central Asian desert into cotton fields. Later, the Aral Sea largely dried up and fields turned salty. How can watering a desert damage it?
About half of the 800-mile Trans-Alaska Pipeline runs above the ground. Why not bury all of it?
Under a salt flat in the Atacama, one of the driest places on Earth, lies brine rich in lithium. Who decides who pumps it?
In 2019 the climb up Uluṟu closed for good, yet the park remains open to visitors. Why close one of Australia's most famous attractions?
Between 11,000 and 5,000 years ago, the Sahara had permanent lakes, plants and people. Today it is desert. Did people cause the change?
Shishmaref, an Iñupiaq village on an Alaskan island, has voted three times to move. Why, and why is it still there?
Deserts get more sunshine than they can use, and many lie beside the sea. Can technology turn sun and seawater into reliable power and water?
option-d-geophysical-hazards: The Atlantic is about 2.5 cm wider every year. What moves the plates?
In 1985 a volcano 45 km away killed about 23,000 people in Armero, two hours after it erupted. How?
The central and eastern USA used to have about 25 earthquakes of magnitude 3 or more a year. In 2015 it had 1,010. What changed?
About 1,600 magnitude-5 earthquakes strike each year, and about one magnitude-8. Which should planners prepare for?
In one Aceh village, the 2004 tsunami killed four females for every male. Why would a wave "choose"?
Nepal 2015 and Kaikōura 2016 were both magnitude 7.8. One killed more than 8,790 people; the other killed 2. Why?
On Fuego, in 2018, a golf resort evacuated safely. A village two kilometres further on was buried. Why?

In 2017 a hillside above Freetown collapsed; about 1,141 people were declared dead or missing. A Californian landslide has been moving since 1956 and is still destroying homes. Are they the same hazard?
Large earthquakes are not becoming more common. So why do experts expect more people to be affected by geophysical disasters?
By 2013, Hong Kong said it had cut the landslide risk from its man-made slopes by about 75%. Is preventing disasters worth more than responding to them?
option-e-leisure-tourism-sport: UK residents made about three times as many trips abroad as Indian nationals did in 2025, yet India has about 21 times as many people. Why?
In England, about 7 in 10 of the most affluent adults are physically active, but only about 5 in 10 of the least affluent. Is money the whole story?
Iceland has about 394,000 people. In 2025 it received about 2.3 million foreign visitors. How did a remote, cold island become a tourism hotspot?

In 1888 all 12 founding clubs of the Football League came from the Midlands and the North of England. In 2026/27, six of the 20 Premier League clubs are in London. What changed, and why does it matter where a stadium is?
For a few days, a dairy farm in Somerset holds more than 200,000 people. Then it goes back to being a farm. Who gains, and who pays?
In 2018, a TV fantasy series helped bring about 1 in 6 of Northern Ireland's out-of-state visitors. Can a country sell a story rather than a place?
Tourism makes up about a fifth of the Maldives' economy. Yet in 2022 most people working in its resorts were not Maldivian. Who really gains from a resort?
France's national audit court says the long-term economic benefits of the Paris 2024 Games are "uncertain". So why do countries still compete to host?
Thailand closed one of its most famous beaches to visitors for about three and a half years. Why would a country shut a beach that tourists love?
In 2017 Rwanda doubled the price of a permit to see mountain gorillas, to US$1,500. Can making tourism more expensive make it more sustainable?
In the first half of 2026, international arrivals in the Middle East fell by more than a fifth. What will shape who travels, and who gets to play sport, in the future?
option-f-food-health: In 2023 the world's food supply came to about 3,000 calories per person per day. So why did around 645 million people go hungry in 2025?
In 2022, 149 million young children were stunted while 2.5 billion adults were overweight. How can the world have too little food and too much at once?
In 2000, non-communicable diseases caused 58% of the world's deaths. In 2023 they caused 74%. Good news or bad news?
Of every 100 calories the world's crops produce, how many reach people's plates as meat, milk or eggs?
By 1980, new high-yielding seeds grew on about 40% of Asia's cereal land; by 2000, about 80%. Why did they spread fast in some places and slowly in others?
Malaria killed an estimated 610,000 people in 2024. Why does it kill mostly in one continent, and mostly young children?
In October 2010, cholera was reported in Haiti. By February 2019 there had been 820,000 cases. How did it arrive, and why did it spread so fast?
From 2016, many packaged foods in Chile carried black "high in" warning labels, with limits on marketing them to children. Did families buy less?
Early warning systems forecast a likely emergency in Somalia in August 2010. Famine was declared in July 2011. Why did a warning not prevent disaster?
Brazil left the UN's Hunger Map in 2014, fell back onto it, then left again in 2025. What does it take to end hunger, and to keep it ended?
New HIV infections have fallen 65% since their peak in 1994. Was that prevention or treatment, and why are some groups still left behind?

In September 2019 a global board warned: "The world is not prepared" for a fast-moving respiratory pandemic. Months later came COVID-19. Why did a warned world still lose an estimated 14.9 million lives in 2020 and 2021?
option-g-urban-environments: In Denmark, 200 people can make a place urban. In Japan it takes 50,000. So how urban is the world?
A square metre of land in Ginza, central Tokyo, is valued at ¥67.1 million. A square metre of housing land in Ome, also in Tokyo, averages ¥98,600. Why the gap?
In 2011, 1 in 10 people in Mumbai's D ward lived in slums. In M/East ward, more than 3 in 4 did. Why such a gap inside one city?
In 1979 Shenzhen was what its government calls "a small backward border town". By 2024 it had 17.98 million residents. Where did they all come from?
Detroit had 1,849,568 people in 1950 and 639,111 in 2020. What emptied the Motor City?
Hong Kong's own reservoirs supply only 20–30% of the water it uses. So how does it have water 24 hours a day?
In 2021 a coroner's report named air pollution exposure as a cause of a 9-year-old London girl's death. Who breathes a city's dirtiest air?
In 2003 London began charging drivers to enter its centre. By 2007 traffic was still lower, but congestion was back where it started. How?
Two neighbourhoods on two continents: both were demolished and redeveloped. Who decides what replaces a neighbourhood?
Singapore's prime minister guessed that protecting the island from rising seas would cost "$100 billion over 100 years". How can a city prepare for risks it cannot stop?
Urban areas use 75% of the world's energy. Vauban, a whole eco-district in Germany, is home to about 5,300 people. Can eco-cities and smart cities make a real difference?
core-unit-1-changing-population: Why do more than 9 in 10 people in China live on one side of a single line?
Is China a rich country or a poor one?
At today's rate, Niger's population would double in about 21 years. Japan's is shrinking. Why?
Dhaka grew from 3 million people in 1980 to over 18 million by 2017. Who gains and who loses when a city grows that fast?
Within a year of August 2017, nearly 725,000 people had fled from Myanmar into Bangladesh. Why do so many people flee at once, and what happens where they arrive?
From 1980 China limited most couples to one child. By 2021 it allowed three. Why the U-turn, and can governments change how many children people have?
Can a falling birth rate make a country richer?
core-unit-2-global-climate-vulnerability: In 1991 one volcano in the Philippines cooled the whole planet. How?
Since 1979 the Arctic has warmed nearly four times as fast as the planet as a whole. Why there?
The UK's emissions fell by 54% between 1990 and 2025. Has the UK really halved its part in climate change?
Global sea level has risen about 10 cm since 1993, and the yearly rise has more than doubled. Where is the extra water coming from?
In June 2021 a Canadian village reached 49.6 °C, a national record. Could that have happened without climate change?
Since the 1950s, many upper-ocean species have moved towards the poles by about 52 km every decade. Why move, and what happens to living things and farms on land?
Rotterdam to Yokohama is about 11,200 nautical miles via Suez, but about 6,500 over the top of the world. Will melting ice make the Arctic a new shipping highway?
About a quarter of the Netherlands lies below sea level. Tuvalu's land averages about 2 m above it. Which is more vulnerable, and why?
The least developed countries emitted less than 0.4% of all historical fossil CO₂, yet face some of the worst impacts. Who should cut emissions, and who should pay?

In May 2024 a company opened what it called the world's largest plant for pulling CO₂ out of the air, in Iceland, designed to capture up to 36,000 tonnes a year. Could machines like it clean up our emissions?

In 2021 Germany's highest court partly upheld complaints against the national climate law brought by people including the very young and some living in Bangladesh and Nepal. How can people outside government change climate action?
core-unit-3-global-resource-consumption-: In 1990, two in three people in East Asia and the Pacific lived in extreme poverty. By 2025, fewer than 1 in 50 did. So why did the number of extremely poor people in sub-Saharan Africa rise?

If everyone lived like the average person in Qatar, humanity would use up a whole year's worth of nature by 4 February. If everyone lived like the average person in India, the year's supply would not run out before the year ended. What is being measured?
Producing 1 kg of beef takes about 15,400 litres of water, on a world average. Is beef draining the world's rivers?
China imported about ten times as many soybeans in 2023 as in 2000. In 2025, nearly three in four came from Brazil. Why does what people eat in China matter to land in Brazil?
In 2025, solar power generation grew by about 30%. In the same year, the world used more fossil fuel than ever. How can both be true?

In March, April and May 2026, oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz averaged about 2.7 million barrels a day, down from about 20 million. Why did farmers and food importers far from the Gulf feel the shock?

Singapore imports more than 90% of its food and makes about 95% of its electricity from imported gas. Jordan has about 61 m³ of renewable water per person a year. Which is more resource-secure, and why?
In 2016, China reported importing about 8.8 million tonnes of plastic waste. In 2018, it imported about 51,000 tonnes. What happened, and where did the waste go?
In 1798, Thomas Malthus argued that population would outrun food. Since 1961, the world's population has grown about 2.6 times. Has food per person risen or fallen?
unit-4-power-places-networks: The Netherlands tops the KOF Globalisation Index. The USA, the world's largest economy at market exchange rates, ranks 28th. How can that be?
In 2025 China's economy was larger than the USA's by one IMF measure and smaller by another. Which country is the superpower?
In 1980 the G7 produced about half the world's output (IMF, at PPP). By 2025 it produced under 30%. Do the old clubs still run the world economy?
In 2022 Sri Lanka defaulted on its foreign debt and turned to the IMF. Who sets the terms of rescue loans, and is there an alternative?
In 2024 one inflow of money into Tajikistan equalled almost half of its GDP. Which flows matter most, and for which places?
Estimated cocaine manufacture more than quadrupled in a decade. How do illegal flows move through a connected world?

Apple employs about 166,000 people. Toyota and its affiliates run more than 50 manufacturing operations in 27 countries and regions outside Japan. Why do these two giants make their products in such different ways?
From 1 January 2021, EU citizens needed points to get a UK work visa. By the year to March 2023, UK net migration had peaked at 944,000. How far can governments control global interactions?
In 2023 the Panama Canal cut the number of ships it let through. In 2026 conflict choked oil shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Has technology really made the world "shrink"?
unit-5-human-development-diversity: Guyana's income per person is more than three and a half times Sri Lanka's. Why do they have exactly the same HDI?
Nearly half of the 2.4 million elected members of India's rural local councils are women. Can reserving places close a development gap?
In 2006 a bank for poor villagers won the Nobel Peace Prize. Do small loans and fairer prices really lift people out of poverty?
After a factory building collapsed in Bangladesh in 2013, more than 200 brands signed a deal to make factories safe. Almost nine years on, how many factories had fixed every problem found?
Nearly half of the world's languages are endangered, yet 4 in 10 Londoners were born abroad. Is the world becoming more alike or more diverse?
There are more than three times as many KFC restaurants in China as in the USA. Why does KFC in China sell rice porridge?
18.5 million people born in India live in other countries, more than from any other country. How do they change places at both ends?
In 2000, after mass protests in Cochabamba, Bolivia, the government cancelled a water contract with a company part-owned by a US TNC. When does local resistance to global forces succeed?
In 2020 Indonesia stopped exporting nickel ore. By 2025 it mined most of the world's nickel. Who gains when a country closes a door?
In 2025 Access Now recorded at least 313 internet shutdowns. Can citizens win back the freedom to connect?
unit-6-global-risks-resilience: On 12 May 2017, at least 81 of England's 236 NHS trusts were disrupted on the same day. Nobody broke into a single building. What happened?

By late January 2024, trade through the Suez Canal had fallen by 42% in two months, while transits of the Panama Canal were down 36% on a year earlier. Why did two canals on opposite sides of the world falter at once?
In 2014, one of Apple's Irish subsidiaries paid tax at an effective rate of 0.005% on its profits. How is that possible, and who loses?
In December 2018, Gatwick Airport grounded its flights for almost 36 hours. Why couldn't the state simply stop the cause?

Between 1970 and 2008 the share of world trade in world GDP more than doubled. Since then it has stalled, moving between about 52% and 62% to 2024, and nationalist politics has grown. Is globalization creating its own backlash?

In September and October 2015, fires in maritime Southeast Asia, mostly in Indonesia, released more CO₂ per day, on average, than all the fossil fuels burned in the European Union. Who pays when one country's smoke crosses borders?
Transporting the world's fruit and vegetables releases almost twice as much greenhouse gas as growing them. So is "buy local" the answer?
In 2006, more than a third of China's sulphur dioxide emissions came from making goods for other countries. Whose pollution is it?

In 2006, a campaign report linked fast-food chains to soy grown on cleared Amazon rainforest. Ten years later, researchers tried to measure what it had changed. Can civil society change how global companies behave?
In 2023, Mexico overtook China as the largest source of the goods the US imports. Is the world "un-globalizing", or rebuilding for resilience?
